title_en: The Allocation Is Agreed. Where Are the Vaccines?
title_zh: 分配表写好了，疫苗在哪里？
deck_en: A delivery in Accra, a shrinking forecast and a later change of method. Fair access needs more than a fair share of what has not yet arrived.
deck_zh: 从阿克拉的一批到货，读到下调的供应预测与后来的办法调整。分得公平，还不等于等得到。
search_labels: COVAX COVID-19 Ghana Accra Gavi CEPI WHO UNICEF vaccine allocation AMC 疫苗 加纳 阿克拉 迦納 全球疫苗免疫联盟 全球疫苗免疫聯盟 新冠
body_zh: 2021年2月24日，六十万剂阿斯利康／牛津新冠疫苗抵达加纳首都阿克拉。疫苗由印度血清研究所生产，前一天从浦那发出。这是COVAX在非洲交付的第一批疫苗。[1]
六十万剂。这个数可以写进运单，可以清点，可以确认飞机已经到达。经历了筹款、谈判和等待之后，一项世界性的合作终于有了一个落地的重量。
只是，到货的新闻还不是接种的记录。机场之后，另有一段路要走。而在这批货到达的同时，其他地方的下一批货，仍然可能只存在于预测中。
COVAX最难的问题，恰好藏在这两个词之间：分配与交付。把现有疫苗分得公平，已经不容易；要让等待分配的疫苗按时出现，还需要另一种本领。
## 先让每个地方都有一份
2020年，疫苗尚在研发，谁会成功、何时获批、能生产多少，都没有定数。共同采购的吸引力不难理解：不必每个国家独自押注某一种候选疫苗，也不必让付不起最高价的地方只能等别人买够。[2]
COVAX不是一个世界卫生政府。它把不同机构的工作接起来：Gavi组织采购与融资机制，CEPI支持研发和相关生产准备，世卫组织提供技术与分配框架，联合国儿童基金会参与采购和交付。生产企业、出资方和各国卫生系统也在其中。合作能把这些环节连接起来，却不会因此把它们变成同一个指挥部。[1][2]
世卫组织2020年的初始框架，设想先按人口比例逐步分配：最初一批以覆盖约3%人口为参照，让医护等优先人群得到保护，再逐步走向覆盖20%人口。20%是初步分配的底线目标，不是全世界接种到这里就该停下来的上限，更不是一张保证某天交货的凭证。[2]
这个办法有一种朴素的说服力。先不要让购买力决定谁能开始。在各地都还缺的时候，至少别让一些地方已经走了很远，另一些地方连起点都摸不到。
但人口比例也会把许多不同的处境暂时放到括号里。医护人员占人口的比重不同，老年人口不同，流行的时间不同，既有的医疗条件也不同。同样一份比例，是让谈判能够开始的办法，不等于现实从此一样。
更重要的是，分配框架只能分配机制能够取得的疫苗。它不能仅凭一张表，就把全球所有生产线、出口决定和已经签下的双边订单都收进来。这里的公平要求，比负责落实它的机构所能支配的范围更大。
这不使要求变得虚假。恰恰相反，它让一个不太悦耳的问题无法绕开：大家同意不该有人被落下，可是，当最早的货已经在别人的合同里，谁有能力把这句话兑现？
## 预测改了，等待不会重新计时
到了2021年9月8日，COVAX的联合声明下调了预期：当时最可能的情形，是全年取得14.25亿剂；原定二十亿剂可供交付的里程碑，则预计推迟到2022年第一季度。这是当时的供应预测，不是后来核算出的全年实际交付量。[3]
同一声明把困难指向富裕国家提早买下供应、出口限制、双边订单被优先履行、扩产和审批延误。它是合作方对处境的公开解释，不能单独替每一份合同判定责任。但这些因素至少说明：分配公式写得正确，货也未必照公式的时间来到。[3]
在事后总结里，推迟常常只是两个日期之间的一道横线。放在一场仍在进行的疫情里，却不是。疫苗晚来以后依然可能有用，但晚来的保护，不会自动补回此前那一段暴露。后来的累计数量，不能把这段时间从故事里删掉。
也不能因此说，所有等待期间的感染与死亡都应算到COVAX头上。疾病传播、国内政策、医疗条件与其他采购渠道共同影响结果。承认时间有代价，不等于已经完成一笔可以逐人结算的因果账。
不过，不能精确结算，不是不用回答。一个接种计划需要安排人员、地点和后续剂次；如果下一批货的时间不断改变，重排计划本身就要花力气。供应方所面对的一次预测调整，到了接收方，可能是一连串必须重新做的决定。这里说的是交付不确定性的实际含义，不是在补写某位护士未经记录的一天。
所以，一剂疫苗的价值不能只用“送到了”来表达。何时到、剩多少有效期、当地能否及时使用，都关系到这次援助到底增加了什么能力。若一种交付只便于发出方清空库存，却把安排不及的风险留给接收方，数字增加了，帮助的分量却未必同比增加。
2021年的联合声明自己就要求捐赠更可预测、数量更稳定、有效期更长。[3]这些要求听起来像物流细节，其实是在问同一件事：谁来承担一份好意落地之前的麻烦？收下物资的人，是否也有条件决定怎样收、什么时候收？
阿克拉的六十万剂因此值得认真记住，不必把它写成一个被后来的困难取消了的开端。货确实到了。也正因为到货是真实的，才更需要把其他尚未到货的承诺从它旁边分出来，不让一个已完成的节点替整条链条报喜。
## 后来不再只是问，还有多少货
到2022年的分配第二阶段，处境已有变化。世卫组织的说明转向更多按参与方需求安排供应，也把来自COVAX之外的疫苗计算在内，考虑各地实际能够使用的数量，并用滚动安排应对不确定性。这不是简单把2020年预想的第二阶段原样执行，而是针对变化后的条件重新调整。[4]
此前担心有人买不到，后来还得担心送来的不是此刻用得上的数量。这两种问题并不互相推翻。稀缺时不能只看谁出价高，供应增多后也不能只看谁愿意发货。要保护人的理由可以保持，落实的办法却需要重看。
把需求听进去，也不等于把问题一概退回给各国：你没有报更多，就是你不需要。表达出来的需求，可能受人员、预算和服务能力限制。一个地方暂时用不了更多疫苗，和那里的人已经得到足够保护，不是一回事。
反过来，外部机构也不能因为担心这些限制，就认定自己总比当地更知道该收多少。帮助补足能力，和代替对方作决定，中间并没有一条靠善意就能跨过去的线。多问一次实际计划，有时比多寄一箱货更接近合作。
人也不能只作为接种率里的一格出现。COVAX AMC在2021年设立了针对符合条件的严重疫苗相关损害的无过错补偿机制，适用于获支持的92个中低收入国家和经济体。它有自己的资格与程序，不是一项覆盖所有健康损失的承诺。[5]
这条途径值得写出来，不能笼统地说个人完全没有申诉或补偿安排。但疫苗损害补偿，回答的也不是同一道问题：为什么一个地方迟迟没有收到原先盼望的疫苗？一个机制解决了某类伤害，不等于其他追问也已有了去处。政府参加合作，同样不能代替每个人对具体接种的知情与同意。
2023年12月，合作方在收尾声明中报告，COVAX已向146个经济体供应近二十亿剂疫苗，并宣布机制将在当月31日结束，相关支持转入常规免疫安排。这是交付剂数，不是二十亿人已经完成接种。[6]
近二十亿剂，不应被一个轻巧的“失败”抹掉。早期的承诺与等待，也不应被一个同样轻巧的“成功”盖住。合作扩大了取得疫苗的可能，仍然没有把购买力、生产能力和决定优先顺序的权力变成一样大。把两件事一起承认，不是各打五十大板，而是不肯让一个总评吞掉经历过的先后。
读到这里，未必需要立刻替COVAX找一个最后的形容词。更值得带走的，也许是一种看分配表的办法：先看它想保护谁，再看它真的能调动什么；看公布了多少，也看哪一部分仍须由别人点头；看总量，还要把时间放回来。
2021年2月24日，六十万剂疫苗抵达阿克拉。这句话可以好好写完。下一句话也应当留着：再下一批，什么时候到？
body_en: On 24 February 2021, a shipment of 600,000 COVID-19 vaccine doses arrived in Accra, Ghana. The AstraZeneca/Oxford vaccine had been manufactured by the Serum Institute of India and dispatched from Pune the previous day. It was COVAX’s first delivery in Africa.[1]

An arrival is a useful place to begin. A shipment has a quantity, a route and a date that can be checked. After the fundraising and negotiations, something that had existed in plans could now be counted in boxes.

But an airport delivery is not a vaccination record. Nor does one completed shipment tell us when the next will come. Those are different achievements, even when a press announcement can make them feel like consecutive frames of the same film.

COVAX brings that distance into focus: the distance between agreeing who should receive something and being able to place it in their hands. Fair allocation is difficult. Obtaining the thing being allocated is another difficulty, governed partly by decisions outside the allocation scheme.
## A share before a bidding war

In 2020, no purchaser knew which vaccine candidates would succeed, when they would be authorized or how much could be manufactured. Pooling purchases offered a way to spread that risk. It also offered countries with less purchasing power something better than waiting until everyone richer had finished shopping.[2]

COVAX was not a world health government. Its machinery connected different organizations: Gavi’s purchasing and financing arrangements, CEPI’s support for development and manufacturing preparation, WHO’s technical and allocation work, and UNICEF’s procurement and delivery role. Governments and manufacturers retained powers of their own. Connecting these actors did not place every decision under a single command.[1][2]

WHO’s initial 2020 framework envisaged proportional allocation, beginning with a benchmark sufficient for roughly 3% of national populations and progressing towards 20%, with priority groups in view. Twenty per cent was an initial floor, not a permanent ceiling on vaccination, and certainly not a guarantee that deliveries would arrive by a particular date.[2]

There was a readily intelligible reason for this approach. Access should not begin only where the strongest buyer had secured the earliest contract. When everyone was short, a country’s ability to start protecting people should not depend entirely on its place in a bidding war.

Population shares nevertheless set aside important differences for the purpose of reaching a workable agreement. Age profiles, health systems and the timing of outbreaks were not identical. A common percentage could make coordination possible without making those differences disappear. It was a starting method, not a final description of equal need.

And the scheme could allocate only what it could obtain. An allocation table did not itself control every manufacturing line, export decision or bilateral purchase. The moral ambition reached further than the partnership’s command over supply. That gap was not an obscure drafting defect. It was central to what the arrangement could deliver.

This does not make the ambition fraudulent. It makes its practical test more demanding. Saying that no country should be left behind remains a reason to act. It does not settle who can obtain doses already promised elsewhere, or what happens when those with the best position in the queue have little incentive to move.
## A revised forecast does not restart the clock

On 8 September 2021, the partnership published a reduced supply forecast. Its most likely scenario was access to 1.425 billion doses that year, with the two-billion-dose milestone for release for delivery postponed to the first quarter of 2022. This was a forecast made at the time, not a subsequently audited total of actual deliveries.[3]

The joint statement identified early purchases by wealthy countries, export restrictions, the prioritization of bilateral deals, production difficulties and regulatory delays. This was the partners’ public account, not an adjudication of liability under each contract. Even so, it showed why an agreed allocation method could coexist with a very different delivery timetable.[3]

In a retrospective chart, a postponement can look like a movement from one column to another. During an epidemic, the interval is not empty. Protection that arrives later may still be valuable. It cannot travel backwards and supply protection during the period when people were waiting.

That observation does not establish that every infection or death during the wait was caused by COVAX. Transmission, domestic policies, health services and other procurement routes also mattered. Acknowledging the cost of time is not the same as possessing a defensible ledger assigning every loss to one organization.

Yet uncertainty about that ledger cannot make the delay irrelevant. Planning vaccination requires staff, sites and arrangements for further doses. When expected supply changes, plans must change too. This is a practical implication of unreliable delivery, not an invented account of a particular nurse’s working day. The inconvenience does not remain where the forecast was revised.

A dose therefore has more than a delivery count. Its arrival date, remaining shelf life and suitability for use affect what help it provides. A donation that is convenient to dispatch can still be difficult to use. If the recipient bears all the risk of a sudden change, generosity in the shipping record need not translate into a comparable gain in usable protection.

The September statement itself asked for more predictable donations with longer shelf lives.[3] Such requests may sound like a retreat from lofty principles into logistics. In fact, they make the principle concrete. Who carries the work created by the gift? Can the receiving health system say when and how it can use what is being offered?

The Accra shipment deserves to remain an achievement. Later shortages did not unmake its arrival. Precisely because it was real, however, it should not be required to stand for every delivery that had not occurred. A completed link in a chain is not evidence that the whole chain has held.
## When the question changes

By the allocation mechanism’s second phase in 2022, conditions had changed. WHO’s explanation moved towards allocations driven more by participant demand, considering supplies obtained outside COVAX, capacity to use doses and rolling arrangements under uncertainty. This was an adaptation to changed circumstances, not simply the execution of every detail envisaged for a later phase in 2020.[4]

Earlier, the urgent problem had been securing scarce supply. Later, it was also necessary to ask whether a proposed delivery matched what could actually be used. These are not contradictory obligations. The reason for protecting people can remain while the way of pursuing it changes. Equal concern need not mean repeating yesterday’s method indefinitely.

Listening to demand, however, cannot mean treating every small request as proof of small need. Staffing, budgets and service capacity can restrict what a country is able to ask for. An inability to use a larger consignment immediately is not evidence that everyone who could benefit is already adequately protected. A demand-led arrangement still needs to hear what makes demand difficult to express.

The converse matters too. An outside organization cannot infer from those constraints that it always knows better than the recipient. Helping a health system do more is different from overruling its plans. Sometimes another conversation about timing is more cooperative than another shipment. Neither a universal formula nor a declaration of local ownership makes that judgment unnecessary.

Individuals must also remain visible. In 2021, the COVAX AMC established a no-fault compensation programme for eligible serious vaccine-related harm in its 92 supported lower-income countries and economies. The programme had eligibility conditions and procedures; it was not a promise to compensate every kind of health loss.[5]

It would therefore be wrong to say there was no individual compensation mechanism at all. But vaccine-injury compensation does not answer a procurement question about a delayed consignment. One route to redress cannot stand in for every other question. A government’s participation likewise cannot supply an individual’s informed agreement to a particular medical intervention.

In December 2023, the partners reported that COVAX had supplied nearly two billion doses to 146 economies. They announced its closure on 31 December, with continuing support moving into regular immunisation arrangements. These were doses delivered, not two billion people who had completed a vaccination course.[6]

Nearly two billion doses should not disappear behind an effortless verdict of failure. Nor should an accumulated total absorb the earlier waiting into an equally effortless verdict of success. Cooperation expanded access without making purchasing power, productive capacity or the power to set priorities equal. Both belong in the account, without being converted into competing points on a scorecard.

The useful question is not which final adjective COVAX deserves. It is how to read an allocation promise: what it aims to protect, what resources it actually commands, which decisions still depend on someone else, and what the calendar means to those awaiting delivery. An aggregate can describe a considerable achievement while leaving important promises unfinished.
On 24 February 2021, 600,000 doses arrived in Accra. That sentence should be allowed to finish. So should the question that follows it: when will the next shipment arrive?
